title: Simon Willison: Engineering practices that make coding agents work - The Pragmatic Summit
summary: Simon Willison describes the practices that make coding agents work: red-green TDD, having agents exercise running code, conformance suites, clean templates, and sandboxing against prompt injection.

assertions.quote: the chances of you getting code that works go up so much if they're if they're if they're writing the test first.

verdicts.note: Tests-first gives agents a target and limits test-cheating; evidence is mostly anecdotal and it does not suit all code (e.g. UI).

assertions.quote: They're free now. They're effectively free.

verdicts.note: AI speeds drafting tests and docs, but generated tests often assert implementation details or weak properties and need review.

assertions.quote: Start the server running um in the background, and then use curl to exercise the API that you just created." And that works.

verdicts.note: End-to-end checks catch integration failures that unit tests miss, a well-established testing principle that applies to agents.

assertions.quote: you can give it to a a good agent and say, "Write code until this test suite passes." And it kind of will.

verdicts.note: Demonstrations such as spec-driven compiler and library ports show agents converge on conformance suites, though code quality can lag.

assertions.quote: If you've got a code base with a bunch of patterns in, they will follow those patterns almost to a T.

verdicts.note: Without enough context, models fall back to common internet patterns; instruction files and indexing reduce but do not remove this.

assertions.quote: there's lots to be said for having for keeping your code base high-quality, because the agent will then add to it in a high-quality way.

verdicts.note: Practitioner reports and agent studies show agents imitate surrounding code and struggle in large messy repos, though controlled evidence is limited.

assertions.quote: having poor quality choice from code from an agent is a choice that you make.

verdicts.note: Linters and agent rules catch local smells, but architecture and coupling decisions still lack automated checks. Tooling is improving.

assertions.quote: nobody writes any code, nobody reads any code, which is clear insanity.

verdicts.note: Ignoring code entirely leads to drift and debt in real codebases; but spec-driven approaches with code review do work.

assertions.quote: there there is no way to reliably say, these are This is the data, and these are the instructions.

verdicts.note: Repeatedly demonstrated against coding agents (malicious repos, issues, docs and MCP tool descriptions causing exfiltration or unsafe commands).

assertions.quote: So, I think the most important thing is sandboxing.

verdicts.note: Agents have deleted files and run destructive commands when unrestricted; vendors themselves recommend containers/VMs for skip-permissions modes.

assertions.quote: the models in November just got so good.

verdicts.note: METR's Feb 2026 update suggests speedups are now likely but its data is unreliable; most evidence is practitioner testimony.

METR Feb 2026: through 2025 agentic tools (Claude Code, Codex) spread, and many experienced OSS developers now refuse to do half their work without AI, which is consistent with a shift; measured speedups remain small and uncertain (-18%, CI -38% to +9%).

assertions.quote: after two hours of that I'm done for the day. Like I'm mentally exhausted

verdicts.note: Many practitioner reports and some surveys describe higher intensity and fatigue from supervising agents, but controlled evidence is thin and other studies report reduced effort on routine work.

assertions.quote: projects are flooded with junk contributions at the moment to the point that people are trying to convince GitHub to disable pull requests

verdicts.note: Maintainers of curl, Ghostty and others document floods of low-effort AI PRs and reports, and GitHub added tooling to restrict PRs in response.
